gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 12 V 100 Ah LiFePO4 battery like WEIZE's lists a 100 A maximum continuous discharge, which is about 1,280 W at 12.8 V, so the 2,000 W inverter in ChatGPT's $999.99 'complete workshop kit' cannot deliver its rated 2,000 W from one battery (2,000 W ÷ 12.8 V ≈ 156 A before inverter losses).
standout_why: I compared against the two cited rivals I could open. ecosolarkits.com explains inverter continuous and surge sizing and gives a current limit (50 A standard, 100 A max) only for the 48 V Sungold battery. It says 'a small kit can have plenty of stored energy and still trip the moment a compressor starts', but it never ties a 12 V 100 Ah battery's BMS current to a 2,000 W inverter. wattfolk.com covers inverter surge and PWM vs MPPT and says nothing about battery discharge current. Both already say LiFePO4 must not charge below freezing without low-temperature protection or self-heating, so the cold-shed fact is not new. agripure.org (cited in chat 1) would not load because of a TLS certificate error, so I could not check it. I did not open the uncited top results (solargenadvisor, kratopower, cleanpowerguide).
kit_items: Power source with battery and inverter in one: BLUETTI AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W continuous AC, 2,700 W Power Lifting for resistive loads only). It avoids the 12 V battery-current cap that limits ChatGPT's WEIZE kit, and BLUETTI sells it as one SKU with a 200 W panel ($769) or two 200 W panels ($1,232).

Solar panel: the BLUETTI 200 W portable panel in the store's AC180+200W bundle. The AC180 accepts 500 W max at 12–60 V and 10 A max, so one 200 W panel is within its limits. A second panel adds more only if wiring keeps current at or under 10 A and Voc at or under 60 V (panel Voc and Isc not sourced).
Placement: the AC180's operating range is 0–40 °C (output drops to 1,500 W at 30–40 °C), so in an unheated shed it has to come indoors in freezing weather. The cited rivals already say this.

findings.note: At 90%, 2,000 W AC needs about 2,222 W DC, or about 174 A at 12.8 V, well above a 100 A BMS. A 100 A BMS therefore supports about 1,150 W AC (1,280 × 0.9).
